title: Attribution: Separating Skill From Exposure
summary: Most of a return is usually explained by what the manager owned rather than by how well they chose it — and proving otherwise takes decades of data.

lesson.body:
[[performance-attribution|Attribution]] asks a single question: **where did this return come from?** The answer splits into three parts that get systematically confused.

**[[beta]] — exposure.** The return earned by holding the risk. A manager who was long equities in a rising market earned it, and so did everyone else who was long equities.

**[[alpha]] — skill.** The return above what the exposure alone would have produced. This is what a fee is supposed to be for.

**Luck.** Random variation, indistinguishable from alpha in any short sample. It is not a residual category to be dismissed — over the horizons people actually assess managers, it is usually the largest of the three.

The basic decomposition uses the exposure to set the benchmark:

**Expected return = risk-free + beta × (market return − risk-free).** Anything above that is alpha.

**The reason this matters commercially: fees are charged on total return and justified by alpha.** If 78% of a return was beta, the investor paid an active fee for a passive outcome — and could have bought the exposure directly for a few [[basis-point|basis points]].

**Distinguishing skill from luck requires far more data than any allocator has, and the required amount is computable.**

The [[information-ratio|information ratio]] is alpha divided by its volatility — how much skill per unit of noise. To establish [[statistical-significance|statistical significance]] at the conventional 95% level, you need roughly **(1.96 / IR)² years** of data:

- **IR 1.0** — exceptional — **4 years**
- **IR 0.5** — very good — **15 years**
- **IR 0.3** — good — **43 years**

**A genuinely good manager with an information ratio of 0.3 requires forty-three years of returns before the record alone can distinguish them from a lucky one.**

Almost nobody has that. Most manager decisions are made on three to five years, which for any realistic information ratio is statistically uninformative about skill.

This is not an argument for giving up. It is an argument for what to rely on instead:

**Process evidence.** How decisions are made, what the edge is, whether it is repeatable in principle.

**Exposure analysis.** What the returns actually correlate with, which is measurable in a short sample even when alpha is not.

**Behaviour in specific conditions.** What they did in the worst quarter and why.

**Consistency of the stated process with the observed positions.** Cheap to check and frequently revealing.

**The honest position: a short track record is evidence about exposures and almost no evidence about skill.** Anyone claiming otherwise is describing a sample, not a manager.

**In alternatives the exposures are harder to see, which makes the beta look like alpha for much longer.**

A [[long-short-equity|long/short equity]] fund's return decomposes reasonably well against equity indices. A buyout fund's does not, and the absence of an obvious benchmark is frequently treated as evidence that the return is skill.

It is not. The exposures are there and they need naming:

**Buyout** — equity beta, leverage, the multiple environment, and a small-cap tilt. A levered small-cap index is a rough but honest benchmark, and it explains a great deal.

**[[private-credit|Private credit]]** — credit beta, illiquidity, and the reference rate. Most of the return is spread that was available to anyone lending on those terms.

**Real estate** — property beta, leverage, and rates. Cap rate compression over a decade of falling rates was not a skill.

**[[hedge-fund|Hedge funds]]** — often equity beta plus short volatility, and both are cheaper to buy directly.

**The specific question that does the most work: what would a passive investor with the same exposures have earned over the same period?** If the answer is close to the manager's return, the fee bought access rather than performance.

**And the alternatives version of the beta problem is worse than in public markets**, because the fee is higher, the term is longer and the benchmark is contested. Which is exactly why the exposure question deserves to be asked before the return question.
A fund returned 12% in a year. The market returned 10%, the [[risk-free-rate|risk-free rate]] was 3%, and the fund's beta to that market is 0.9.
walkthrough: So of the 12% delivered, **9.30 percentage points — 78% of the return — was beta**, and 2.70 points was alpha.
**Read that carefully: a manager who beat the market by two points added 2.70% of value, and 78% of what the investor received was available passively.**
Now the significance question. Suppose the alpha's volatility is 9%, giving an information ratio of 0.3. Years required = (1.96 / 0.3)² = **43**.
One year of 2.70% alpha is consistent with genuine skill and equally consistent with noise. **The data cannot tell, and it will not be able to tell for four decades.**
Which means the fee discussion is really about the 2.70%: what is a fair price for an alpha that cannot be verified within a career?
Sanity check worth reusing: **compute beta × market return before looking at anything else.** It gives the passive equivalent immediately, and the gap is the only part that requires a manager.

lesson.body:
**Benchmarks chosen after the fact.** A manager compared with a benchmark selected once returns are known will beat it. Ask when the benchmark was set and by whom.

**Beta measured against the wrong market.** A small-cap growth fund benchmarked to a broad index will show alpha that is entirely style exposure.

**Alpha from illiquidity.** Earning a premium for accepting illiquidity is a real return and it is compensation for a constraint rather than skill — and it is available to anyone willing to accept the same constraint.

**Survivorship in a peer group.** Comparisons against a universe of surviving funds flatter everyone in it, because the failures are missing.

**Asymmetric attribution.** Good years explained by process, bad years by the environment. It is the most reliable single diagnostic of a manager who has not separated the two.

**Fee comparison on gross returns.** Alpha net of fees is what the investor keeps, and a strategy with genuine gross alpha and higher fees can be worse than a cheaper passive exposure.

**Once the return is decomposed, the fee conversation changes from "is this expensive?" to "what is this fee being charged on?"**

Take the worked example: 12% delivered, 9.30% of it beta, 2.70% alpha. On a 2-and-20 structure the fee is charged against the whole 12%.

So the arithmetic is stark. **The [[management-fee|management fee]] alone consumes most of the alpha, and the performance fee takes a fifth of a return that was three-quarters passive.** That is not necessarily unreasonable — access, diligence and operational infrastructure cost money — but it should be stated in those terms rather than as a share of performance.

Three questions follow, all answerable:

**Is the fee charged on total return or on return above a benchmark?** A performance fee over a cash hurdle in a rising equity market pays for beta. A fee over an appropriate index pays for alpha.

**What would the same exposure have cost passively?** For most alternatives there is an approximate passive equivalent, and the difference is the price of the access and the alpha together.

**Is the alpha large enough to survive the fee?** Gross alpha of 2.70% against fees of 2% plus 20% of everything leaves very little, and that calculation is arithmetic rather than opinion.

**The best-structured funds address this directly** — benchmark-relative performance fees, hurdles set above cash, [[fee-offset|fee offsets]]. Those are structural answers, and their presence or absence tells you what the manager thinks they are selling.

**Compute beta × market return first.** It gives the passive equivalent in one line, and the residual is the only part that needed a manager.

**Ask (1.96 / IR)² for the manager's information ratio.** It converts "strong track record" into the number of years required before the record means anything.

**Ask when the benchmark was chosen and by whom.** After-the-fact benchmarks are the most common way alpha is manufactured.

**For buyouts, insist on attribution to EBITDA growth, debt paydown and multiple change.** Only the first two are plausibly attributable to the manager.

**Ask what a passive investor with the same exposures would have earned.** If the answer is close, the fee bought access — which may be worth paying for and should be named accurately.

items: Return splits into beta, alpha and luck. In the worked example 78% of a 12% return was beta and 2.70 points was alpha.
Proving skill needs (1.96 / IR)² years: 4 years at an information ratio of 1.0, 15 at 0.5, and 43 at 0.3. Most decisions are made on three to five.
A short record is evidence about exposures and almost none about skill — so rely on exposure analysis, process, and behaviour in the worst quarter.
In alternatives the exposures are harder to see, which makes beta look like alpha for longer. Ask what a passive investor with the same exposures would have earned.

questions.stem: A return decomposes into three components. Which one is a fee supposed to be paying for?
choices: Beta — the return from holding the exposure
Alpha — the return above what the exposure alone would have produced
Luck — random variation in a short sample
rationales: Beta is available passively for a few basis points, so paying an active fee for it is paying for packaging.
Correct. Alpha is the part that required a manager. Whether it can be distinguished from luck in a short record is the harder question.
Luck cannot be bought or sold, and in short samples it is usually the largest of the three.
Fees are charged on total return, which is precisely the problem the decomposition exposes.
questions.explanation: The gap between what a fee is charged on and what it is justified by is the whole fee debate. Decomposing the return first turns it from an argument about value into an arithmetic comparison.

questions.stem: A fund returned 12%. The market returned 10%, the risk-free rate is 3% and the fund's beta is 0.9. What is alpha, in percent? Two decimal places.
questions.explanation: The beta contribution of 9.30% is 78% of what the investor received. That split is the entire fee argument, and it takes one line to compute from data every factsheet already contains.

questions.stem: A manager has an information ratio of 0.3. Roughly how many years of returns are needed for 95% statistical significance? Round to the nearest year.
questions.explanation: Forty-three years for a genuinely good manager. It is the most sobering calculation in manager selection, and it explains why process evidence and exposure analysis have to carry the weight that the track record cannot.

questions.stem: A fund was long equities through a rising market and returned 15%. What does this establish about the manager's skill?
choices: That the manager has strong stock-picking ability
Very little — most of the return is explained by the exposure, and skill is whatever remains after accounting for it
That the manager should be paid a performance fee
That the fund's beta must be greater than 1
rationales: Anyone long equities earned a return in that market. The interesting quantity is what was earned above that.
Correct. Decompose first: the beta contribution is available passively, and only the residual required a manager.
A performance fee on a return that was mostly beta pays for the exposure, which is the problem the decomposition exposes.
Beta could be anything; nothing in the description determines it.
questions.explanation: This is why the first calculation on any return is beta times market return. It costs nothing, uses data already on the factsheet, and it reframes the entire conversation from performance to exposure.

questions.stem: "Five years of top-quartile returns is strong evidence of skill." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — for realistic information ratios, five years is statistically uninformative about skill; it is evidence about the exposures the manager held
False — track records are entirely meaningless
True — five years is the industry standard evaluation period for good reason
False — because quartile rankings are computed incorrectly
rationales: Correct. At an information ratio of 0.5 you need fifteen years, and at 0.3 you need forty-three. Five years cannot separate skill from a favourable environment.
Over-correction. Returns are informative about exposures, style and behaviour — just not about skill at conventional confidence levels.
It is the standard because it is available, not because it is sufficient.
Ranking methodology is a secondary issue; survivorship in the peer universe is a bigger one.
questions.explanation: The constructive response is to use the five years for what it can support: decomposing exposures, examining the worst quarter, and checking that positions match the stated process. Those conclusions are available from a short sample, and skill is not.

questions.stem: A buyout fund reports a 20% IRR over a decade of falling interest rates and rising multiples. What is the key attribution question?
choices: How much of the return came from EBITDA growth and debt paydown, versus multiple expansion the manager did not create
What was the average holding period
rationales: Deal count describes activity rather than the source of the return.
Correct. Multiple expansion is a market condition available to every buyer in that period, and it is not repeatable on demand. Only the first two components are plausibly attributable to the manager.
Holding period affects the IRR mechanically and does not separate the components.
Size affects capacity and strategy rather than attribution.
questions.explanation: The follow-up is the one that settles it: what is the return assuming exit at the entry multiple? Any manager underwriting honestly already has that figure, because it is the standard conservative case — and its absence is itself informative.

questions.stem: A fund delivers 12% of which 2.70% is alpha, charging 2% management and 20% of total return. What does the decomposition reveal?
choices: The fee is reasonable because the fund beat the market
The management fee alone consumes most of the alpha, and the performance fee is charged on a return that was three-quarters beta
The fee is irrelevant since returns are reported net
rationales: Beating the market by two points is the gross alpha, and the fee is levied on the whole return rather than on that part.
Correct. 2% against 2.70% of alpha leaves very little, and 20% of 12% is charged on a return that was mostly available passively.
Net reporting shows the outcome and conceals what the fee was charged on, which is the question here.
The arithmetic points the other way.
questions.explanation: This is why fee structure matters more than fee level: a performance fee over an appropriate benchmark rather than over cash charges for alpha rather than for exposure. The presence or absence of that feature tells you what the manager believes they are selling.
